column1: “The new tax law will take money from my bank account.”
column2: That's false. Government and tax officials have said clearly that no one's account will be debited. Banks only report accounts with very large flows, about ₦25 million in a quarter. Ordinary savers aren't affected.
column3: Tax reform chair (now Finance Minister) Taiwo Oyedele; the Nigeria Revenue Service also denied the claim.

column1: “The new tax laws punish the poor.”
column2: It's the opposite for low earners. If you earn ₦800,000 a year or less, you pay no income tax at all. Basic food, education, healthcare and rent carry no VAT. Higher earners pay more, and the top rate of 25% only applies above ₦50 million a year.
column3: Nigeria Tax Act 2025, in force since 1 January 2026.

column1: “The new tax law will kill small businesses.”
column2: Small businesses are protected. A company with turnover of ₦100 million or less is exempt from company income tax and doesn't have to charge VAT. The goal is to tax big players fairly and stop harassing small traders.
column3: Exemption also requires fixed assets under ₦250 million.

column1: “Now they're charging VAT on bank transfers.”
column2: No. The money you transfer or withdraw is not taxed. VAT on bank fees and charges has always existed; the new law didn't add it. The tax service corrected that rumour in January 2026.

column1: What are the new tax laws, and when did they start?
column2: Four laws signed 26 June 2025: the Nigeria Tax Act, Tax Administration Act, Nigeria Revenue Service Act and Joint Revenue Board Act. The main personal tax changes took effect on 1 January 2026.
column3: Don't say "nobody will pay more tax": higher earners do.
